questions.question: What is the difference between @Mock and @Spy in Mockito?
questions.title: @Mock vs @Spy Mockito | Java Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: @Mock creates a fully fake object where all methods return default values (null, 0, false) unless stubbed. @Spy wraps a real object instance where unstubbed methods call the real implementation; only configured methods are overridden. Use @Spy when you need partial mocking of a real object.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of Mockito's core annotation differences and when to apply each in real test scenarios
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using @Spy everywhere thinking it's safer, or using @Mock when you actually need some real behavior to execute
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that @Spy is particularly useful for testing legacy services where you want real logic but need to intercept specific external calls like database queries

sections.title: Mock vs Spy: Two Approaches to Test Isolation
sections.content: When writing unit tests, you often need to replace dependencies with test doubles. **@Mock** creates a completely fake object from scratch—every method returns a default value (null for objects, 0 for numbers, false for booleans) unless you explicitly stub it with `when().thenReturn()`. Think of it like a **mannequin in a store window**—it looks like a person but doesn't do anything real. **@Spy** wraps an actual instance of your class—unstubbed methods execute the real code, and you only override specific methods you need to control. It's like a **stunt double in a movie**—the real actor does most scenes, but the double steps in for dangerous parts. The key decision: do you need ANY real behavior (use @Spy) or NONE (use @Mock)?

sections.title: Choosing Between Mock and Spy
sections.content: Use **@Mock** when you want complete control and isolation—testing a service class where you don't care about the real repository logic, only that it returns specific test data. This is the default choice for 90% of unit tests. Use **@Spy** when you need the real implementation to run but want to intercept specific methods—for example, testing an OrderService where most methods work fine, but you want to fake the email notification call to avoid sending real emails. A classic scenario: you have a legacy class with 15 methods and only need to stub 2 of them—@Spy lets you avoid stubbing all 13 others. Warning: if you find yourself using @Spy frequently, it often signals that your class has too many responsibilities and should be refactored.

sections.title: Mock vs Spy in a Service Test
Key Points
content: **@Mock**: creates a hollow object where every method returns default values unless explicitly stubbed with when().thenReturn()
**@Spy**: wraps a real instance so unstubbed methods execute the actual implementation code
**Stubbing syntax difference**: use doReturn().when(spy) with spies to avoid calling the real method during setup
**Default choice**: prefer @Mock for clean unit tests with full isolation; use @Spy only when you need real behavior
**Verification**: both support verify() to assert method calls, but @Spy verifications apply to the real wrapped object
**Initialization**: @Mock works with just the annotation; @Spy requires an initialized instance or @Spy annotation on a field with initialization
**Performance**: @Mock is lighter since no real code runs; @Spy incurs the cost of executing real methods

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: At-Mock creates a fully fake object where all methods return defaults like null or zero unless you stub them. At-Spy wraps a real instance, so unstubbed methods actually run the real code. Here's a concrete example: if you're testing an OrderService, you'd use at-Mock for the repository because you don't want real database calls—you just want to return test data. But if that OrderService has an internal method that does complex validation logic you DO want to test, you could use at-Spy on the OrderService itself and only stub the database call part. The big gotcha with at-Spy is that when you stub a method, you have to use doReturn dot when syntax instead of when dot thenReturn, otherwise Mockito calls the real method during setup which can throw exceptions or cause side effects. In practice, I'd reach for at-Mock by default for cleaner tests with full isolation, and only use at-Spy when I specifically need some real behavior to run, like testing a legacy class where refactoring isn't an option right now.

questions.question: What is a test double and what are the different types?
questions.title: Test Double Types | Java Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: Test doubles are fake objects that replace real dependencies in unit tests to provide isolation. The five types are Dummy (unused placeholder), Stub (returns canned data), Fake (simplified working implementation), Mock (records and verifies calls), and Spy (wraps real object with selective stubbing).

interviewer_intent.testing: Precise vocabulary around test doubles and understanding that mock is not a catch-all term
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Calling everything a mock when they're actually using stubs or fakes, showing imprecise thinking
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Reference Gerard Meszaros who defined these terms, and map each type to its Mockito or Spring Test equivalent with concrete examples

sections.title: Test Doubles: Five Tools for Test Isolation
sections.content: In unit testing, you rarely want to test a class with all its real dependencies—databases are slow, external APIs are unreliable, and email services send actual emails. **Test doubles** are fake objects that stand in for real dependencies, giving you control and speed. Think of them like **stunt doubles in filmmaking**—each type serves a different purpose depending on what the scene needs. Gerard Meszaros formalized five types in his book *xUnit Test Patterns*: Dummy, Stub, Fake, Mock, and Spy. Many developers incorrectly call everything a mock, but each type has distinct behavior. A **Dummy** is passed around but never used. A **Stub** returns hardcoded values. A **Fake** has working logic but simplified (like an in-memory database). A **Mock** records interactions and verifies them. A **Spy** wraps a real object and selectively overrides methods. Understanding these distinctions makes you a more precise tester.

sections.title: Five Test Double Types in Practice
Key Points
content: **Dummy**: object passed to satisfy a parameter but never actually used in the test—often just null or an empty object
**Stub**: returns pre-programmed responses to calls—created with when().thenReturn() in Mockito
**Fake**: has a working but simplified implementation like H2 in-memory database or a HashMap-backed repository
**Mock**: records method calls and verifies interactions happened—created with @Mock and verified with verify()
**Spy**: wraps a real object instance allowing real methods to run but selective stubbing of specific methods
**Terminology precision**: saying mock when you mean stub shows lack of depth—use the correct term for the behavior you need
**Mockito mapping**: @Mock creates both stubs (when you stub) and mocks (when you verify); @Spy creates spies; Fakes you write manually

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Test doubles are fake objects that replace real dependencies in unit tests so you don't hit actual databases or external services. There are five types, and it's important to use the right terminology. A Dummy is just a placeholder you pass to satisfy a method signature but never actually use—sometimes you just pass null. A Stub returns hardcoded values, like when you use Mockito's when dot thenReturn to make a repository return a specific test order. A Fake is a real working implementation but simplified—like using an H2 in-memory database instead of PostgreSQL in tests, or writing a HashMap-backed fake repository. A Mock is what Mockito creates when you want to verify that specific methods were called—you use verify to assert interactions happened. A Spy wraps a real object so most methods run the real code, but you can selectively stub specific methods. The common mistake is calling everything a mock—that shows you don't really understand the distinctions. If I'm testing an OrderService, I'd use a stub for the repository to return test data, maybe a fake in-memory cache, and a mock for the email service to verify sendConfirmation was called. Gerard Meszaros defined these terms in his testing book, and knowing them makes you sound a lot more precise in interviews.

questions.question: What is @InjectMocks in Mockito and how does it work?
questions.title: @InjectMocks Mockito Java | Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: @InjectMocks creates an instance of the class under test and automatically injects @Mock and @Spy dependencies into it. It tries constructor injection first, then setter injection, then field injection. This eliminates manual instantiation like new OrderService(mockRepo, mockEmail) in every test method.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical knowledge of Mockito test setup automation and dependency injection strategy
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Forgetting @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class) which enables the annotation, or not understanding that injection silently fails if no matching strategy works
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the three-phase injection strategy and the silent failure gotcha—if injection fails, @InjectMocks just creates the object with nulls for dependencies

sections.title: Automatic Dependency Injection for Tests
sections.content: Writing unit tests often requires creating the class under test and wiring in mock dependencies. Without **@InjectMocks**, you'd write `new OrderService(mockRepo, mockEmail)` in every test setup, which is tedious and brittle—add a new dependency and every test breaks. **@InjectMocks** automates this wiring by scanning the test class for @Mock and @Spy fields and injecting them into the target object. Think of it like **Spring's @Autowired but for tests**—Mockito handles the plumbing so you focus on test logic. It tries three strategies in order: **constructor injection** (creates object via constructor), **setter injection** (calls setters), and **field injection** (directly sets private fields). The gotcha: if none of these strategies work, @InjectMocks silently creates the object with null dependencies, causing NullPointerExceptions in your tests. You must use @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class) to activate the annotation processor.

sections.title: InjectMocks with Constructor Injection
Key Points
content: **@InjectMocks**: creates an instance of the class under test and automatically injects @Mock and @Spy fields as dependencies
**@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)**: required JUnit 5 annotation to enable Mockito annotations including @InjectMocks
**Constructor injection**: preferred strategy—Mockito looks for a constructor matching the mock types and calls it
**Setter injection**: fallback if no constructor matches—calls setXxx methods for each mock field
**Field injection**: last resort—directly sets private fields via reflection when no constructor or setter exists
**Silent failure gotcha**: if no injection strategy works, @InjectMocks creates the object with null dependencies causing NullPointerException in tests
**Best practice**: design classes with constructor injection for real code—it makes @InjectMocks work reliably and supports immutability

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: At-InjectMocks creates an instance of the class you're testing and automatically wires in any at-Mock or at-Spy fields from your test class. It saves you from writing new OrderService with all the mock parameters in every test. Mockito tries three strategies in order: first it looks for a constructor that matches the mock types and calls it, which is the cleanest approach. If there's no matching constructor, it tries setter methods like setRepository. As a last resort, it uses reflection to directly set private fields. The key thing is you must have at-ExtendWith with MockitoExtension dot class at the class level, otherwise the annotations don't do anything. A gotcha I've hit: if none of the injection strategies work, Mockito silently creates the object with null dependencies instead of failing the test, so you get NullPointerException when the test runs. To avoid this, design your production classes with constructor injection, which is also a Spring best practice. So in an interview, I'd say at-InjectMocks handles the boilerplate of creating the test object and wiring dependencies, it uses constructor injection preferably, and you need the MockitoExtension to make it work.

questions.question: How do you use doReturn().when() vs when().thenReturn() in Mockito?
questions.title: doReturn vs when thenReturn Mockito | Java Fresher
questions.direct_answer: Both stub methods, but doReturn().when() avoids calling the real method during setup. For @Mock objects, both syntaxes work identically. For @Spy objects, when().thenReturn() calls the real method before stubbing it, which can trigger side effects or exceptions. Always use doReturn().when() with spies.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of Mockito's subtle API differences and when each syntax is appropriate for mocks vs spies
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using when().thenReturn() on a @Spy and accidentally executing the real method during test setup, causing unexpected behavior
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the execution sequence: when(spy.method()) invokes the real method to record the invocation before thenReturn applies the stub

sections.title: Two Stubbing Syntaxes with Different Execution Timing
sections.content: Mockito provides two syntaxes for stubbing method calls: **when().thenReturn()** and **doReturn().when()**. For @Mock objects, they're functionally identical—both stub the method without calling real code. But for **@Spy objects**, there's a critical difference. The `when(spy.method())` syntax **evaluates the method call immediately** to record it for stubbing, which means the real implementation runs during test setup. Think of it like **setting a trap that triggers before you finish setting it**. The `doReturn().when(spy).method()` syntax uses method references and **never calls the real method**, making it safe for spies. This difference matters when the real method has side effects (writes to a database, sends an email) or throws exceptions (validates inputs that don't exist yet). Always use doReturn().when() with spies to avoid these problems.

sections.title: Choosing the Right Stubbing Syntax
sections.content: Use **when().thenReturn()** as your default for @Mock objects—it's more readable and type-safe. The natural method call syntax `when(repo.findById(1L)).thenReturn(order)` is easier for other developers to understand. Use **doReturn().when()** in three scenarios: (1) stubbing methods on @Spy objects to avoid calling the real method during setup, (2) stubbing void methods where you need doNothing() or doThrow(), and (3) when you need to stub the same method multiple times with consecutive calls using doReturn().doReturn().when(). The trade-off: doReturn().when() sacrifices compile-time type checking—the compiler can't verify that your return value matches the method's return type, so you might only catch mistakes at runtime. In practice, for @Mock use when().thenReturn() for clarity, but for @Spy always use doReturn().when() to prevent accidental real method execution.

sections.title: Demonstrating the Difference with Spy
Key Points
content: **when().thenReturn()**: natural readable syntax that evaluates the method call immediately to record the invocation
**doReturn().when()**: reverse syntax using method reference that never executes the real method
**@Mock objects**: both syntaxes work identically since there's no real implementation to call
**@Spy objects**: must use doReturn().when() to avoid triggering real method logic during test setup
**Void methods**: when().then() doesn't work syntactically; must use doNothing() or doThrow() with the do-family syntax
**Type safety trade-off**: when().thenReturn() has compile-time return type checking; doReturn() accepts any object and checks at runtime
**Consecutive calls**: use doReturn(val1).doReturn(val2).when() to stub multiple return values for the same method

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Both when dot thenReturn and doReturn dot when stub methods in Mockito, but they differ in when the method gets called. For at-Mock objects, they work the same—neither calls real code. But for at-Spy objects, there's a critical difference. When you write when spy dot method then return, Mockito actually calls the real method right there during setup to record the invocation. If that method has side effects like database writes or throws an exception, your test setup fails. The doReturn dot when syntax uses a method reference so the real method never runs. Here's a concrete example: if you're spying on a PaymentValidator and stub validateCard with an invalid card number, using when dot thenReturn would call the real validateCard which might throw an exception before you even finish setting up the stub. Using doReturn dot when avoids this completely. The other use case is void methods—you can't stub them with when dot then because there's no return value, so you have to use doNothing dot when or doThrow dot when. In practice, I'd use when dot thenReturn for mocks because it's more readable, but always switch to doReturn dot when for spies to be safe.

questions.question: When would you use a Spy instead of a Mock?
questions.title: When to Use a Spy
questions.direct_answer: Use a Spy when you want the real methods of an object to execute by default, but you need to selectively stub or verify specific methods. This is useful for partial mocking scenarios like testing legacy code where most methods should run normally but you need to fake external dependencies.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding that Spy enables partial mocking and when that's the right tool versus full isolation with Mock
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using Spy as a default thinking it's more realistic, when most unit tests should use full Mocks for complete isolation
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that doReturn().when() must be used with Spy to avoid calling the real method during stubbing setup

sections.title: Partial Mocking with Spy
sections.content: A **Spy** wraps a real instance of a class and allows most methods to run their actual implementation while you selectively override specific methods. It's the opposite of a **Mock**, which fakes everything by default. Think of testing a **Swiss Army knife**—you want to test that the blade works (real method), but you don't want the corkscrew to actually open a bottle (stubbed method). Spies are useful in three scenarios: (1) **legacy code** where a large class has many methods and refactoring isn't feasible, so you stub only the problematic dependencies; (2) **integration-style tests** where you want to test real logic but fake external systems like email or payment gateways; (3) **self-calls within a class** where one public method calls another and you want to verify the interaction. The danger: overusing Spy often indicates poor class design with too many responsibilities—if you need to stub half the methods, that class should probably be split.

sections.title: Step 1: Determine if Real Behavior Is Needed
sections.content: Ask yourself: do I need ANY methods to run their real implementation? If the answer is no—you want complete isolation and control—use @Mock instead. For example, testing an OrderService that depends on a repository: you don't want any real database logic, so @Mock is perfect. But if you're testing that same OrderService and it has an internal calculateDiscount() method with complex logic you DO want to test, but you need to fake the database call, then @Spy the OrderService itself. The key indicator: if you're only stubbing 1-3 methods out of many, Spy makes sense. If you're stubbing most methods, you're fighting the tool—use Mock.

sections.title: Step 2: Remember the doReturn().when() Requirement
sections.content: When you decide to use @Spy, you must change your stubbing syntax from when().thenReturn() to doReturn().when(). This is because when(spy.method()) calls the real method to record the invocation before applying the stub. If that real method throws an exception or has side effects, your test setup fails before the test even runs. Use doReturn(value).when(spy).method(args) to safely stub without triggering real code. For example, doReturn(fakeOrder).when(spyService).fetchFromDatabase(1L) stubs the database call without actually hitting the database during setup. This syntax is less intuitive but necessary for Spy safety.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **Spy use case**: partial mocking where most methods run real code but specific methods are stubbed or verified
**Legacy code scenario**: testing a large class where refactoring isn't feasible and you need to fake only external dependencies
**Real instance required**: @Spy wraps an actual object instance, so you must initialize it either inline or in @BeforeEach
**doReturn().when() syntax**: required for stubbing Spy methods to avoid calling the real method during test setup
**Self-call verification**: Spy lets you verify when one method in a class calls another method in the same class
**Design smell**: frequent Spy usage indicates classes with too many responsibilities that should be refactored into smaller, focused classes
**Performance cost**: Spy executes real methods so it's slower than Mock; prefer Mock for pure unit test speed

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: You'd use a Spy when you want most of the methods in a class to run their real implementation, but you need to selectively stub or verify specific methods. This is called partial mocking. A concrete example: imagine testing an OrderService that has 10 methods including some complex business logic you DO want to test, but it also calls a database repository and an email service you DON'T want to actually invoke. You could at-Spy the OrderService so the business logic runs for real, then stub just the database and email methods. The critical thing with Spy is you have to use doReturn dot when syntax instead of when dot thenReturn to stub methods, because when dot thenReturn actually calls the real method during setup which defeats the purpose. Another use case is legacy code—you inherit a 500-line service class that you can't easily refactor, so you Spy it and stub just the external calls to third-party APIs. But honestly, if you find yourself using Spy a lot, it's a design smell. It usually means your classes are doing too much and should be broken up so you can test them with clean Mocks instead. In most unit tests, I'd default to at-Mock for full isolation and only reach for at-Spy when I have a specific reason to run some real code.

questions.question: What is a Fake object and how does it differ from a Mock?
questions.title: Fake Object vs Mock
questions.direct_answer: A Fake is a working implementation with simplified logic used for testing, like an H2 in-memory database or a HashMap-backed repository. A Mock is a framework-generated test double that verifies method calls and returns stubbed values. Fakes have real behavior; Mocks have expectation-based verification.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding the broader test double vocabulary beyond what Mockito provides and when to write custom Fakes
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing Fakes with Mocks because both are test objects, missing that Fakes implement real logic while Mocks only verify interactions
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give concrete examples like H2 for database Fakes or writing a simple in-memory fake repository class for tests

sections.title: Fake: Real Logic, Simplified Implementation
sections.content: A **Fake** is a test double you write yourself that has a working implementation but takes shortcuts for simplicity. Think of it as a **bicycle version of a car**—it gets you from A to B but without the complexity of an engine. The classic example: using **H2 in-memory database** instead of PostgreSQL in tests—H2 is a real database that executes SQL, but it runs in memory so it's fast and doesn't require setup. Another example: writing a **FakeOrderRepository** backed by a HashMap instead of hitting a real database table. A **Mock**, in contrast, is generated by Mockito and has no real logic—it just records method calls and returns stubbed values. Mocks focus on **interaction verification** (was this method called?), while Fakes focus on **state verification** (did the data change correctly?). You use Fakes when you need realistic behavior that's too complex to stub method-by-method, but you don't want the overhead of the real implementation.

sections.title: Fake vs Mock Implementation
Key Points
content: **Fake**: test double you write yourself with real working logic but simplified for testing (like HashMap instead of database)
**Mock**: framework-generated object that records method calls and returns stubbed values for interaction verification
**H2 database**: the most common Fake in Java tests—a real in-memory database replacing PostgreSQL or MySQL
**State verification**: Fakes are tested by checking the data state after operations (did the order get saved?)
**Interaction verification**: Mocks are tested with verify() to assert specific methods were called with expected arguments
**When to use Fake**: when behavior is too complex to stub method-by-method but you need realistic logic without production overhead
**When to use Mock**: when you only care about verifying method calls happened, not the actual data transformation logic

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: A Fake is a working implementation that you write yourself with simplified logic for testing, while a Mock is generated by Mockito and just records method calls without any real behavior. The best example is database testing: H2 is a Fake—it's a real in-memory database that actually executes SQL and stores data, but it's simpler and faster than PostgreSQL. You could also write a FakeOrderRepository class backed by a HashMap that implements the repository interface with real save and find methods. In contrast, a Mock would be created with at-Mock annotation and you'd stub methods like when repo dot save then return some order. The Fake actually runs logic and transforms state, so you verify it by checking the data changed correctly. A Mock has no logic at all—you verify it by calling verify to assert that methods were called. You'd use a Fake when the behavior is too complex to stub method-by-method, like a repository with complex query logic, or when you want tests that feel more like integration tests but still run fast. Mocks are better for unit tests where you only care about verifying that one service called another service with the right parameters, not about the actual data transformation. In a Spring Boot test, you might use H2 as a Fake database but at-Mock the external email service since you just want to verify sendEmail was called.

questions.question: What is the difference between @SpyBean and @MockBean in a Spring Boot test?
questions.title: @SpyBean vs @MockBean in Spring Boot
questions.direct_answer: @MockBean replaces a Spring bean in the application context with a full Mockito mock where all methods return defaults. @SpyBean wraps the real Spring bean instance so unstubbed methods run the actual implementation. Both dirty the Spring context, forcing a reload for each test class that uses them.

interviewer_intent.testing: Knowledge of Spring Boot test annotations and their integration with Mockito, plus understanding of application context lifecycle
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using @MockBean when only one method needs stubbing, causing unnecessary full mocking and context reloads
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that both annotations dirty the Spring context, causing performance degradation in large test suites, and suggest @MockBean for external dependencies only

sections.title: Spring-Aware Mocking with Context Integration
sections.content: **@MockBean** and **@SpyBean** are Spring Boot test annotations that bridge Mockito with the Spring application context. Unlike plain @Mock and @Spy which work outside Spring, these annotations replace or wrap beans that are already managed by Spring. Think of **@MockBean** like **replacing a part in a running machine**—Spring's context has a UserRepository bean, but @MockBean swaps it with a Mockito mock so any component that @Autowires UserRepository gets your mock instead. **@SpyBean** wraps the real bean—the original Spring-managed object still exists, but Mockito intercepts calls so you can stub specific methods while letting others execute normally. The critical difference from plain @Mock: both annotations modify the Spring context, which triggers a **context reload** if another test class has different @MockBean/@SpyBean configurations. This can severely impact test suite performance, so use them only for integration tests, not unit tests.

sections.title: Choosing MockBean vs SpyBean
sections.content: Use **@MockBean** when testing a Spring slice (like @WebMvcTest or @DataJpaTest) and you need to fake an external dependency that the test slice doesn't provide. For example, @WebMvcTest loads only the web layer, so if your controller uses a service, you @MockBean that service. Use @MockBean for repositories in controller tests, or external REST clients—anything you don't want real behavior from. Use **@SpyBean** rarely, only when you need a real Spring bean but must intercept specific methods—like testing a service that autowires a complex validator and you want the validator's real logic except for one external API call. Key performance consideration: every unique combination of @MockBean/@SpyBean configurations creates a new application context. If Test A mocks the UserRepository and Test B mocks the OrderRepository, Spring loads the context twice. This adds 2-5 seconds per unique context. To minimize this, group tests with the same @MockBean setup in one class, or prefer unit tests with plain @Mock which don't involve Spring at all.

sections.title: MockBean vs SpyBean in a Spring Test
Key Points
content: **@MockBean**: replaces a Spring-managed bean with a Mockito mock in the application context
**@SpyBean**: wraps a real Spring-managed bean with a Mockito spy allowing partial stubbing
**Context dirtying**: both annotations modify the Spring context, forcing a reload if configurations differ across test classes
**Performance impact**: each unique @MockBean/@SpyBean combination creates a new context, adding 2-5 seconds per reload
**@WebMvcTest use case**: mock the service layer with @MockBean since @WebMvcTest only loads controllers
**@DataJpaTest use case**: typically don't need @MockBean since the test slice provides a real database (H2)
**Best practice**: minimize @MockBean/@SpyBean usage—prefer unit tests with plain @Mock for speed, reserve @MockBean for integration tests

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: At-MockBean replaces a Spring bean in the application context with a full Mockito mock, while at-SpyBean wraps the real Spring bean so real methods run unless you stub them. The key difference from plain at-Mock is these work with Spring's dependency injection—any component that autowires the bean gets your mock or spy. Here's a practical example: if you're writing a web layer test with at-WebMvcTest, you'd use at-MockBean for the service layer since WebMvcTest doesn't load services, only controllers. The mock service goes into the context and gets injected into your controller automatically. You'd use at-SpyBean less often, maybe when testing a service that autowires a complex component and you need most of its real logic but want to fake one external API call. The critical performance gotcha is both annotations dirty the Spring context. If TestA mocks the UserRepository and TestB mocks the OrderRepository, Spring reloads the entire context twice, which can add several seconds per unique configuration. That's why you should prefer plain at-Mock for unit tests and only use at-MockBean for integration tests where you actually need Spring's context. In an interview, I'd say at-MockBean is for faking external dependencies in Spring test slices, at-SpyBean is for partial mocking of real Spring beans, and both come with a context reload cost you should be aware of.

questions.question: Can you spy on a final class or a static method in Mockito, and how?
questions.title: Mocking Final Classes and Static Methods
questions.direct_answer: Yes, Mockito 2.x introduced the inline mock maker that can mock final classes and methods, and since Mockito 3.4.0 you can use mockStatic() to stub static methods. However, heavy reliance on these features often indicates design problems—prefer refactoring to use dependency injection or wrapper classes instead.

interviewer_intent.testing: Awareness of Mockito's extended capabilities beyond basic mocking and the design implications of needing them
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking Mockito can never mock final or static, missing the inline mock maker feature introduced in Mockito 2.x
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that while technically possible, mocking statics is often a code smell and suggest dependency injection or wrapper patterns as better solutions

sections.title: Extended Mocking with the Inline Mock Maker
sections.content: Early versions of Mockito used bytecode generation via CGLIB, which couldn't mock **final classes** or **static methods** because Java doesn't allow subclassing final classes or overriding static methods. **Mockito 2.x** introduced the **inline mock maker** that uses Java instrumentation to rewrite bytecode at runtime, removing these limitations. You can now mock and spy on final classes without any special configuration—just use @Mock as normal. For static methods, **Mockito 3.4.0** added `mockStatic()` which creates a scoped mock that intercepts static calls within a try-with-resources block. Think of it like **opening a portal into a parallel universe** where that static method behaves differently, then closing the portal when you're done. However, needing to mock statics often signals a **design problem**—static methods create tight coupling and make code hard to test. The better solution is usually to **wrap the static call in an injectable service** or refactor to use instance methods instead.

sections.title: Mocking Final Classes and Static Methods
Key Points
content: **Inline mock maker**: introduced in Mockito 2.x, uses Java instrumentation instead of CGLIB to enable mocking final classes
**Final class mocking**: works automatically with @Mock annotation—no configuration needed since Mockito 2.x
**Static method mocking**: requires mockStatic() in try-with-resources block, available since Mockito 3.4.0
**Scoped static mock**: mockStatic() only affects code within the try block—auto-restores when block exits
**Design smell**: frequently mocking statics indicates tight coupling and poor dependency injection
**Better alternatives**: wrap static calls in an injectable service class, or refactor to use instance methods with dependency injection
**Performance cost**: static mocking uses thread-local state and is slower than regular mocking—avoid in tight loops

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Yes, Mockito can mock final classes since version 2.x when they introduced the inline mock maker. Before that, Mockito used CGLIB which creates subclasses, and you can't subclass a final class in Java. The inline mock maker uses Java instrumentation to rewrite bytecode at runtime, so final is no longer a barrier. You just use at-Mock normally and it works. For static methods, Mockito added mockStatic since version 3.4.0. You use it in a try-with-resources block to create a scoped mock—within that block, calls to the static method return your stubbed value, and when the block exits, the static method goes back to normal behavior. Here's a concrete example: if you're testing code that calls LocalDateTime dot now, you can use mockStatic with TimeUtils dot class to return a fixed time for deterministic tests. But honestly, if you find yourself mocking statics a lot, it's usually a design smell. Static methods create tight coupling and make testing hard. The better solution is to wrap the static call in an injectable service—create a ClockService with a now method that you can mock normally. Or refactor to use instance methods with dependency injection instead of statics. So in an interview, I'd say yes Mockito can technically do it, but I'd also mention that needing to mock statics often means the code should be refactored for better testability.
